title: test-0090-SOC-GEO-MOTIONS
passage: The Earth is always in motion, performing two distinct types of movement. First, it spins on its own invisible axis, which is an imaginary line connecting the North and South Poles. This rotation takes about 24 hours to complete, creating the cycle of day and night as different parts of the planet face the Sun. While spinning, the Earth also travels around the Sun in a fixed path called an orbit. This journey, known as revolution, takes approximately 365 and a quarter days. Because we cannot easily count a quarter day every year, we add one extra day to our calendar every four years, creating a leap year. The Earth’s axis is tilted at an angle of 23.5 degrees. This tilt is the primary reason for our changing seasons. As the Earth revolves, different hemispheres receive varying amounts of direct sunlight. When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, it experiences summer, regardless of whether the Earth is at its closest or farthest point in its orbit. The distance between the Earth and the Sun does not determine the season; rather, it is the angle of the sunlight hitting the surface that makes the weather warmer or cooler throughout the year.
summary: When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, it gets summer, even if the Earth is closest or farthest from the Sun. The distance between the Earth and the Sun does not determine the season; rather, it is the angle of the sunlight hitting the surface that makes the weather warmer or cooler throughout the year.
